question.worked_solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3x})}^{2(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $3x=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{3x+1}{3x})}^{6x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{3x})}^{2(3x)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{2n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{2} \\  & ={e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$
